topic: managing the cutting rotation of a firewood coppice and drying the split wood

provenance.author: glowny-en-e
provenance.notes: 10 turns, user first; variant a is a closed arithmetic tally of a firewood order (panels, cords, bearers, loads, hours) with one closed task question per turn, base is a diagnosis of wood coming in wet. Grounded external referent: the stack behind the barn that holds the split wood, named in turn 0 and again immediately before every insertion, and it stays one of the two suspects to the end.

a: Work through the firewood order for the coppice, taking the five panels one at a time.
Panel one yields twelve cords and panel two yields nine cords of split wood.
Panel three yields seven cords, while panel four yields five cords on the same sheet.
Panel five is the smallest of the five, with three cords beside the track.
Set the panels out from largest to smallest, and state the total reached after each one.
How many cords does the whole cut come to once the five have been added?
base: The firewood off our own coppice has burned badly for two winters and the stove tars up.
We cut one panel each January and split the wood before the end of March.
The split wood then goes onto the stack behind the barn for a summer and a winter.
The stack takes only about four cords, so the rest sits under the trees where it fell.
Where would you start looking for the reason so much of it still comes in wet?

a: Set out largest first, the order runs panel one, panel two, panel three, panel four, panel five.
The totals reached after each panel are twelve, then twenty-one, then twenty-eight cords.
The last two totals are thirty-three and then thirty-six cords across the whole cut.
At four hours of splitting to the cord that comes to one hundred forty-four hours.
Does the total of thirty-six cords match the figure written on the order sheet?
base: The stack is the first thing I would look at, because a shaded wall dries nothing.
Split ash needs sun and a through wind, and a north wall gives neither of them.
Wood left under the trees will still be near thirty percent water by the autumn.
A meter reading on a fresh face at the stack would tell you where you stand.
Do you measure the wood at all before it comes in for the stove?

a: Now work out the bearers, at six bearers for every cord stacked behind the barn.
Give the bearer count for all five panels in the order you set them out.
Sheets cover four cords each, and every panel starts a fresh sheet of its own.
Put panels one and two on the first stack, and the other three on the second.
Which bearer count belongs to panel four at that fixed rate per cord?
base: We measure nothing, and the wood comes in by the barrow as the shed empties.
The stack stands against the north wall and it has been there since my father's day.
We cut the panel in January and the poles lie whole until the middle of March.
The rounds go through the splitter in one long weekend and then straight onto the pile.
Would moving the whole stack out into the open be enough on its own?

a: Panel one takes seventy-two bearers and panel two takes fifty-four bearers at that same rate.
Panel three takes forty-two bearers, and panel four takes thirty bearers of the same length.
Panel five takes eighteen bearers, which is the smallest figure anywhere on the whole sheet.
The first stack therefore needs one hundred twenty-six bearers for the two panels going on it.
Does the bearer total of two hundred sixteen agree with the count kept in the barn book?
base: Moving it will help, though an open stack needs a roof or the rain undoes the summer.
What you want is sun on one face and wind through the rows, not a sheltered corner.
I would build the stack on bearers with a sheet over the top and nothing else.
Cutting in January is right, but leaving the poles whole until March wastes the best weeks.
How long does the panel take you from the first pole to the last split round?

a: One correction before we go on: panel three yields eight cords and not seven.
Redo its bearers and its sheets, and leave the other four panels exactly as they stand.
Then give the new totals for cords and for bearers across the whole cut.
After that list the five panels in the order the crew will work them this winter.
Which panel comes first under the order panel two, panel five, panel one, panel four, panel three?
base: The panel takes us about six weekends, and the splitter comes out only at the end.
The rotation runs on twelve years, which is what my father worked to as well.
Nobody has changed that figure in years, and the stack has stood in the same corner throughout.
The poles are thicker than they used to be and the deer take the young shoots hard.
Could a longer rotation be costing us more than it gives us in the end?

a: Panel three at eight cords now takes forty-eight bearers and two sheets of its own.
The new cord total is thirty-seven across the five panels of the whole coppice.
The new bearer total comes to two hundred twenty-two for the work this winter.
The splitting time rises to one hundred forty-eight hours at four hours a cord.
Does the working order still open with panel two exactly as it was set out?
base: Twelve years grows heavy poles, and heavy ash takes two summers rather than one to dry.
A shorter rotation of eight years gives thinner poles that split and dry far faster.
Browsing is the bigger worry, since a browsed stool throws weak shoots for years.
I would fence the panel for the first four seasons and cut it at eight.
How many panels do you have in the wood as it stands today?

a: Turn the whole cut into loads for the trailer, at three cords to the load.
Tell me how many full loads that needs and how many cords are left over.
Then split the bearer total between two barns of equal share, and give each figure.
The crew starts at eight in the morning and splits one cord every four hours.
How many full loads does a total of thirty-seven cords come to?
base: There are twelve panels in all, and we take them in order round the wood.
We could fence one panel a year if the posts come out of the same cut.
The stack behind the barn takes four cords, though, and a thinner pole gives more of them.
Stacking two years of wood at once would mean rows too deep for the wind.
Would a deep row spoil the drying we are trying to gain here?

a: Thirty-seven cords make twelve full loads for the trailer with one cord left standing over.
Each of the two barns takes one hundred eleven bearers for its own rows of wood.
Panel two takes thirty-six hours of splitting, and panel five takes twelve hours after it.
Panel one takes forty-eight hours of work across the coldest part of the winter.
Panel four takes twenty hours and panel three takes thirty-two hours, closing the whole cut.
base: A deep row will spoil it, because the middle stays damp right through the summer.
Keep every row one length wide and leave a good gap between the rows.
Better still, split the wood into two stacks so both faces catch the wind.
Cut, split and stack within the same six weeks so the wood starts drying early.
Mark each row with the year of the cut so nothing goes in the stove too soon.

a: Print a short list of the four steps in order for the crew this winter.
Step one is felling, step two is snedding and step three is cutting to length.
Step four is splitting, and each step needs the clock time for panel two.
Felling starts at eight in the morning and the splitting finishes at four exactly.
Which clock time closes the snedding if felling and snedding take two hours each?
base: That sounds workable, and two stacks cost us nothing but a few more bearers.
I will paint the year on the end of each row so the boys take the older one.
One worry is the fencing, which will eat into the wood we cut for the stove.
If every post comes out of the panel we will lose a cord a year.
Should the posts come from the thinnings instead of the standing poles?

a: Step one is the felling at eight, and it runs two hours on that panel.
Step two is the snedding from ten until twelve, exactly as you set it out.
Step three is the cutting between twelve and two on the very same panel.
Step four is the splitting from two until four, which closes panel two.
Panel five follows at four, and that order holds for the rest of the week.
base: Yes, take the posts from the thinnings and leave the straight poles for the stove.
Thinnings make short posts, and a browsing fence needs only four feet of height.
Set the fence in the spring after the cut and lift it once the shoots harden.
Then the same posts go round the next panel and the wood loses nothing at all.
Three or four years of that and the stove should draw clean all winter.
